# Tobit Chapter 12 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Codex Sinaiticus, Tobit 12 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/TOB_012_page_001.jpg

---

**1** Old Tobit called his son Tobias aside and said, "Now, my son — make sure you pay the man who traveled with you what he's owed. Give him more than you promised."

**2** Tobias answered, "Father, how much should I give him? I'd gladly give him half of everything he helped me bring home —

**3** because he brought me there and back safely, he healed my wife, he recovered the silver, and on top of all that, he healed you too."

**4** The old man nodded. "He deserves every bit of half of it."

**5** So Tobit called Azariah in and said, "Take half of everything you helped bring back. Go well, friend."

**6** Then Raphael drew them both aside, privately, and spoke: "Praise God. Thank him before everyone — tell the world what he has done for you, so they too will bless and praise his name. Shout God's deeds from the rooftops. Never stop being grateful.

**7** A king's secrets you keep quiet — but God's works? Those you proclaim. Loudly. Gloriously. Do what is right, and disaster will never find you.

**8** Prayer combined with fasting is powerful. Giving to those in need — giving out of a just heart — that is worth more than mountains of gold. Better to give away a little rightly than to hoard a fortune wrongly.

**9** Because giving mercy saves you from death. It washes away every sin. Those who are merciful, who live justly — they will be filled with life.

**10** But those who choose evil? They become their own enemies.

**11** "I can't keep the truth from you any longer. I said there are secrets worth keeping — a king's business, yes. But God's business? That must be told.

**12** So here it is: when you prayed, Tobit — when you and your daughter-in-law Sarah both cried out to God — I carried your prayers before the Holy One. I stood in his presence with them.

**13** Every time you got up from dinner to go bury one of the dead — every act of faithfulness — I saw it. And I was sent to test you, to see if you were real.

**14** But God also sent me for another purpose: to heal you, and to heal Sarah.

**15** I am Raphael. I am one of the seven holy angels who stand in the presence of God, who carry the prayers of his people before the Glory of the Holy One."

**16** They collapsed. Both of them — flat on their faces, trembling with terror.

**17** But Raphael said, "Get up. Don't be afraid. Peace be with you. Bless God forever —

**18** because I didn't come to you on my own initiative. I came by the will of your God. Praise him every day of your lives. Never stop.

**19** "And the eating you saw — that wasn't really eating. What you saw was a vision.

**20** Now give thanks to God. I am returning to the one who sent me. Write all of this down — every single thing that happened."

**21** They stood up. He was gone. They couldn't see him anywhere.

**22** They broke into praise. They sang. They thanked God with everything in them for these staggering wonders — because an angel of God had appeared to them in the flesh.

---
## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

This is one of the most extraordinary angelophany scenes in ancient literature. Raphael's unveiling in v. 15 has no close parallel in the Hebrew Bible — he names himself, names his rank, names his function (intercessory presence before God), and explains the entire preceding narrative. The drama I've tried to capture is the whiplash: these two ordinary people discover that their traveling companion was an archangel all along.

The triad in v. 8 (prayer + fasting + almsgiving) is the moral heart of the book. It's not just piety — it's the theology of *eleēmosyna* as a cosmic force that literally reverses death. I've rendered it with ascending urgency.

Verse 19's "vision" clarification is theologically daring. The author doesn't want readers to think angels eat — Raphael says plainly it was appearance, not reality. I preserve this honesty rather than smoothing it.

The ending (v. 22) is quiet after all that thunder. Two old people praising God in an empty room. That's the image the chapter ends on.

— PNEUMA
